caseStudies.title: I build the repos our teams use to design with AI
caseStudies.summary: Our designers were prototyping in Figma and their own separate repos, and nobody could build on anyone else's work. I proposed one shared repo, built it, and still own it. It's now required for designers across multiple teams, and PMs and engineers work in it too. I've since built several more, and hundreds of people use them.

facts.Ownership: I proposed it, built it, and own the architecture and roadmap
facts.Collaboration: My design manager, designers, PMs, and engineers
facts.Scope: The prototyping workflow for multiple teams
facts.Status: Required for designers. Engineering handoff is in progress.
facts.Evidence: Internal use. Diagrams redrawn with generic labels.

outcomes.label: Designers, PMs, and engineers using the repos I've built
The standard way our designers prototype
Used for ideation, demos, customer concepts, and handoff

caseStudies.title: I turned a requirements maze into an agent that starts from your PRD
caseStudies.summary: Every PM had to dig through a wiki, fill out a form, track down contacts, and create work by hand. In a three-day Microsoft hackathon, I built a package of skills and workflows that starts from the PM's PRD instead. The agent pulls out what it can, asks about the rest, and gives the PM a report to check. Nothing else happens until the PM says so.

facts.Role: Senior Content Designer. It was my idea, and I drove it.
facts.Ownership: The skills and workflows, most of the agent instructions, the full interaction, and the demo video
facts.Team: Three people: me, another designer, and a product manager
facts.Status: Proof of concept, now part of a larger PM system that's still growing
facts.Evidence: Best Use of AI, judges' feedback, and wide sharing across PMs. Examples are redrawn with generic content.

outcomes.label: Best Use of AI, for our three-person team
From idea to working proof of concept
Across the PM org, and fed into its skills and agents

caseStudies.title: How I got my design org actually using AI
caseStudies.summary: I didn't wait for an AI strategy. Three times I spotted something missing, took it to leadership, drove it from proof of concept to required workflow, and trained the people using it. That's a content-design agent, a shared knowledge base, and training across the org.

facts.Role: Senior Content Designer. I led the efforts, own the KB review process, train across the org, and wrote the playbook articles and prompt collections people learn from.
facts.Scope: A design org with multiple teams in multiple countries
facts.Pattern: Spot the gap, get leadership on board, build a v-team, prove it, ship it, make it required
facts.Status: All three are active and required
facts.Collaboration: Senior org leaders, principal design managers, DesignOps, repository owners, reviewers, and subject-matter experts
facts.Evidence: Internal adoption, VP-level recognition, and an internal showcase talk

outcomes.label: Designers using the content-design agent I created
Efforts I took from idea to required workflow
Of the review process for the org's shared knowledge base

caseStudies.title: I built the AI skills that shipped with Fabric CLI
caseStudies.summary: People were already using AI assistants to run the Fabric CLI, but the assistants didn't understand Fabric, and everyone was writing their own instructions. Before GA, I proposed a shared set of AI assets, shaped it with the PM, and wrote it: agent context, a custom mode, a prompt, skills, references, and scripts. It's all public.

facts.Ownership: I proposed it, designed it, and wrote the files in my PRs
facts.Collaboration: The Fabric CLI PM and engineering team
facts.Status: Shipped at GA. The public repo has kept changing since.
facts.Evidence: Public PRs, commits, release notes, and the GA article

outcomes.label: Shipped with Fabric CLI at GA
In my main AI assets pull request
PRs, release notes, and a launch article I co-wrote

caseStudies.title: Research, writing rules, and UI copy for a history game
caseStudies.summary: I have a background in history, so I started contributing to Statecraft: Israel, an open-source strategy game. I researched the history with sources, turned it into game data, wrote guidance and AI skills for other contributors, and rewrote player-facing copy. So far that's 20 merged pull requests.

facts.Role: Contributor: historical research, writing guidance, and UX writing
facts.Contribution: I found the gaps, proposed fixes in public issues, and wrote 20 merged PRs
facts.Scope: Contributor guidance, AI skills, research, game data, UI copy, localization guidance, and release notes
facts.Collaboration: The project owner, maintainers, and other contributors
facts.Evidence: Public issues, PRs, reviews, tests, and contributor credit

outcomes.label: For research, writing, UX copy, and video scripts

caseStudies.title: I pitched Wix’s first accessibility checker and helped turn it into a product
caseStudies.summary: Wix had no accessibility tool. I took an idea people were talking about, built it on the editor’s existing SEO checker, and led a hackathon team to a working demo. That demo got us in front of the CEO, which led to funding, a dedicated product team, and an accessibility checker that shipped inside the Wix editor.

facts.Role: Concept lead and team lead, then UX writer on the product team
facts.Team: Designers, product marketers, and one PM. I led it.
facts.Ownership: The concept, the pitch, the demo, and the CEO presentation
facts.Timeline: A hackathon, then six months on the new product team
facts.Outcome: Shipped in the Wix editor as its accessibility checker

outcomes.label: Accessibility tool in the Wix editor

As the product team’s UX writer, alongside my Wix Code work

headline: Hi, I’m Jeremy. I design AI systems and developer tools: content, AI workflows, and product experiences that connect design, product, and engineering.
about: I design customer-facing developer tools, content experiences, and product workflows, as well as internal systems that teams depend on. At Microsoft Fabric, my work spans content and product design for CI/CD, CLI, and MCP experiences. I also own the design automation repo our 30-person design and PM team uses, a system I built from scratch that saw immediate adoption and now supports everything from daily prototyping to senior leadership demos.

My background is unusual for someone doing this work. I started in journalism and history, moved into content and UX writing, and kept pushing further into the technical side until I was building agentic workflows, shipping skills to production, and contributing to open-source Microsoft tooling. I think that path is a feature: I bridge the human side of product problems with the technical side of building systems.

On top of that, I've driven org-wide AI initiatives at Microsoft. I initiated a content design agent that was adopted and used by 150+ designers, and I was a key contributor to the Fabric CLI's AI assets layer, the part the Corporate VP of Product highlighted when it shipped GA. I'm also an instructor at the UX Content Collective, where I created the Technical Content Designer program.

I'm part of Content Design Leaders Upstream, an invite-only workgroup shaping what UX content becomes in an AI-driven world. We compare active fieldwork and build frameworks the broader field can use.
